messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Vignette:
Diego was 22 when he came to treatment, a single Latin American man working as a product manager, with a polished, high-responsibility job that required him to spend long hours in front of a laptop and in meetings that he now found difficult to follow without scanning the room. A year earlier, while living in a city that had become increasingly unstable around him, he had been caught in the middle of armed conflict as a civilian. He had not been a soldier or a target in any direct sense, but he had learned quickly that ordinary routines no longer protected anyone. On the day that stayed with him, he was outside a small grocery store when a burst of gunfire sent people running in different directions. Someone shouted for everyone to get down. Diego remembered the hard pavement against his body, the sound of boots and voices moving too fast, and the terrible uncertainty of not knowing where the shots were coming from. What remained most vivid was the sensation in his own body: every muscle locked, his chest tight, his whole frame braced for impact. Since then, he had come to experience his body as if it were perpetually on the edge of that moment.

In the weeks after the event, Diego found himself living as though danger might appear at any second. He watched doorways, street corners, and the movement of strangers with a level of alertness that made simple errands exhausting. In public places he kept track of who was behind him and who had moved suddenly in his peripheral vision. Unexpected movement nearby could make him jerk before he had time to think, his body reacting as if the same violence were about to unfold again. Even now, in the open-plan office where he worked, a coworker passing too quickly behind his chair or a hand reaching across the conference table could make his shoulders shoot upward and his attention snap sharply away from the discussion. He described feeling constantly tense, as though his body were “stuck ready,” unable to settle fully even when nothing was happening.

Over time, Diego began checking his body repeatedly for signs that he was injured or in danger. After the chaos in the war zone, he found himself paying close attention to every sensation: a twitch, a racing pulse, a soreness in his side. He would run his hands over his arms and ribs, looking for wounds that were not there, and he often paused in the bathroom at work to inspect himself in the mirror. These checks had become part of his daily routine, especially when he felt startled or when he remembered the gunfire. He was not reassured for long, and he would soon be looking again. At the same time, he kept asking people around him to tell him he was okay. Friends, roommates, and later colleagues heard him say things like, “Do I look normal?” or “You’d tell me if something was wrong, right?” He seemed to need repeated confirmation that his body was intact and that he was not silently in immediate danger. The asking could become urgent, especially after a movement or noise had caught him off guard, and it left him feeling embarrassed, but he did it anyway because the alternative felt worse to him.

There were also moments when the strain became so intense that he hurt himself physically to release what he experienced as overwhelming pressure inside. He spoke about these episodes reluctantly, saying only that when everything felt too tight and unbearable, causing pain in his own body could make the feelings let up for a while. He did not describe this as wanting to die; rather, he described it as trying to get some relief from a state that felt uncontainable. Those moments were frightening in a different way, because they left him with shame afterward and a renewed wish to make sure nothing was seriously wrong with him.

At work, Diego had managed to keep performing, but his concentration was frequently interrupted by the need to scan the room or check his own body. In meetings, he sometimes missed parts of conversations because he was watching a chair scrape back or a colleague shift quickly in his seat. He had become more careful about where he sat, preferring positions where he could see the entrance and the people moving around him. Outside of work, he had gradually narrowed his routines, choosing routes and places that felt easier to monitor, though he could not always avoid the uneasy feeling that danger might arrive from nowhere. He said he was tired of feeling as if his own body were always telling him to prepare for something he could not see.

What finally brought Diego to seek help was the combination of exhaustion, the embarrassment of continuing to ask for reassurance, and the growing fear that he could not keep living in this state of constant readiness. He wanted to stop reacting so sharply to movement and to stop checking himself over and over, but he was most afraid that if he let his guard down, something would happen and he would miss it. At the same time, he was hoping that treatment might help him feel less trapped in his own body and more able to move through his work and daily life without feeling as though danger were only a second away.
